subject: Sparse autoencoder feature geometry as a probe for cross-layer concept binding in superposition regimes

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-562)
response:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on individual layers decompose residual stream activations into approximately monosemantic features, but the central question here is whether the geometric relationships among those features — angles, norms, co-activation structure — carry information about how the model binds together concept components that are co-represented across multiple layers simultaneously. In superposition, a layer encodes more features than it has dimensions by exploiting near-orthogonality, so a single neuron's activation is a lossy projection of many features; the worry is that an SAE trained on layer L recovers features that are artifacts of the superposition geometry at L rather than stable conceptual units that the model actually uses to propagate bound representations forward. The binding problem here is sharp: if "Paris" as a capital and "Paris" as a French city are partially represented in layer 8 and partially in layer 14, no single-layer SAE sees the full binding, and the inter-layer feature geometry — how the layer-8 Paris-capital direction relates to the layer-14 Paris-city direction under the model's residual stream transport — is precisely what a cross-layer probe needs to recover. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is interference from privileged basis effects and from SAE training incentives: the L1 sparsity penalty pushes the SAE toward solutions that minimize reconstruction loss greedily per layer, which can split a single cross-layer concept into multiple spurious per-layer features that look clean individually but don't correspond to any coherent computational unit the model uses. The deeper concern is that "feature geometry" as measured by cosine similarity in the SAE basis may be confounded by the decoder weight norms and the specific random seed of SAE training, making apparent cross-layer alignment look meaningful when it's actually an artifact of how two separately trained SAEs happened to tile the same high-dimensional space.

Empirically, SAE features show moderate but imperfect seed-to-seed stability: work from the Anthropic interpretability team and independent replications on GPT-2-scale models finds that the most active, highest-frequency features (think "starts a new sentence" or "is inside a Python function") recover reliably across seeds with decoder cosine similarities above 0.9, but the long tail of low-frequency, polysemantic features often fragments differently — one seed splits a concept into two features where another seed merges them, with cosine similarities in the 0.3–0.6 range for matched pairs. This instability is not random noise: it tracks feature load, meaning how many ground-truth concepts are crowded into a region of activation space, so seeds disagree most precisely where superposition is densest. For cross-layer alignment, this creates a compounding problem — if layer-L features are seed-unstable at rate ε₁ and layer-L' features at rate ε₂, then a cross-layer cosine similarity between two SAE decoder directions inherits both instabilities, and you cannot distinguish "these two layers encode the same concept" from "these two SAEs happened to tile adjacent superposition regions similarly." The concrete diagnostic is a seed-ensemble alignment matrix: train k SAEs per layer, compute all k² cross-seed cosine similarity matrices within a layer, and use the rank of the stable matched subspace (features with mean pairwise cosine > 0.85 across seeds) as a mask before doing any cross-layer comparison — features outside that stable subspace should be treated as SAE artifacts, not model features. What instability tells you is precisely that cross-layer feature alignment is only trustworthy in the high-frequency, low-superposition regime, which is unfortunately not where the interesting concept-binding phenomena live; the binding of rare or context-specific concepts is exactly what falls into the unstable tail.

response:
Using the Jacobian as a transport operator is conceptually cleaner than raw decoder cosine comparison because it respects the model's actual computation: if feature f at layer L has decoder direction d_L, then J·d_L gives you the first-order prediction of how that feature's activation perturbs the layer L+1 residual stream, which you can then project onto the layer L+1 SAE dictionary to get a "transported feature" and ask which L+1 features it most activates. This approach has been explored in the context of path patching and attribution work (Nanda et al., Conmy et al. on ACDC, and implicitly in Elhage et al.'s mathematical framework for transformers), and it does buy you something real: features that are computationally continuous across layers — where the model is genuinely propagating the same representation — will show high overlap between J·d_L and the matched L+1 decoder direction, while features that are recomputed at L+1 from attention over other tokens will show low overlap, which is a meaningful distinction that raw cosine similarity misses entirely. The breakdown when using an input-specific Jacobian is severe: the Jacobian of a transformer layer includes contributions from the attention pattern, which is input-dependent, so J computed on "The Eiffel Tower is in Paris" has a completely different attention-weighted mixing matrix than J on "Marie Curie was born in Warsaw" — meaning the transported feature direction is not a property of the feature but of the feature in that context, and averaging across inputs to get a "mean Jacobian" destroys exactly the structured variation you care about for concept binding, which is inherently context-sensitive. A deeper problem is that the Jacobian is only a first-order approximation, and in layers where LayerNorm, ReLU-family activations (like GeLU in GPT-2/GPT-4 class models), or attention softmax introduce significant curvature, the linear transport can be badly wrong for feature directions that don't lie near the linearization point — empirically this shows up as J·d_L having high norm but low SAE reconstruction quality at layer L+1, a sign the transported direction has left the manifold the SAE was trained on. The honest conclusion is that the Jacobian approach gives you a more mechanistically interpretable notion of cross-layer identity but trades one problem (SAE geometry artifacts) for another (input-conditioned transport), and the most defensible use is to restrict it to attention-head outputs where the transport is closer to linear and to use a distribution of Jacobians clustered by attention pattern type rather than a single input or naive average.

Yes, and this is one of the most underappreciated architectural gaps in current SAE work: standard SAEs are trained on individual (token, layer) activation vectors, which means they can only recover features that are localized to a single residual stream slice, but binding phenomena like coreference ("she" bound to "Marie Curie" twenty tokens back), syntactic agreement, or multi-token entity recognition are by construction distributed across token positions and only become visible when you treat the full (seq_len × d_model) tensor as the object of analysis. The implication is that a per-token SAE will systematically misattribute binding features: the "Marie Curie" entity representation at the pronoun token position will look like a freestanding semantic feature to a per-token SAE, with no structural signal that it was assembled via attention from an earlier position, because the assembly mechanism is in the attention weights, not in the residual stream vector itself. Some recent work gestures at this — the "attention SAE" direction explored informally in the Anthropic interpretability ecosystem and more explicitly in work on sparse attribution over attention patterns — but a genuine solution requires SAEs defined over attention-pattern-weighted combinations of residual stream vectors, effectively encoding features as functions of (query position, key position, d_model) triples rather than single vectors, which is a much higher-dimensional and computationally expensive object. The architectural implication is sharp: you'd need either a factored SAE that separately encodes "what is being bound" (content directions in d_model) and "where the binding reaches" (attention head routing across seq_len), or a set-based encoder that takes the full attended context as input — neither of which has a clean sparsity penalty because L1 on a structured object like an attention-weighted sum doesn't decompose the way it does for a single vector. The practical warning is that any empirical claim about cross-layer feature geometry for binding phenomena made using standard per-token SAEs is likely measuring the residue of binding in the current token's residual stream after attention has already mixed positions, which is a downstream shadow of the actual binding operation rather than the operation itself — analogous to trying to understand addition by only looking at the output register.

response:
The cleanest distinguishing test is causal intervention under positional scrambling: take a corpus of sentences where the semantic relationship holds but the typical positional configuration is violated — coreference across unusual distances, subject-verb agreement with heavy center-embedding, entity binding where the antecedent appears after the pronoun (as in "Before she spoke, Marie Curie checked her notes") — and ask whether the factored SAE feature activates on the semantic relationship regardless of positional signature, or whether it drops out when the usual n-gram positional statistics are disrupted. A genuine binding feature should show high activation on semantically matched pairs across varied positional configurations, while a positional artifact will activate on the typical distance/position pattern even when the semantic relationship is absent — you can construct minimal pairs by swapping content words to break coreference while preserving position, which is the factored-SAE analogue of the behavioral tests used in BERT probing literature (e.g., Hewitt & Manning 2019 on structural probes, or Ravfogel et al. on causal interventions in probing). A second test is activation under meaning-preserving paraphrase with different surface structure: if "The scientist who won the prize accepted it graciously" and "She won the prize; the scientist accepted it graciously" activate the same factored feature at the (pronoun-query, antecedent-key) position pair despite completely different token distances and syntactic paths, that's strong evidence for semantic grounding rather than positional artifact. The worry an expert has that a beginner misses is that transformers trained on natural language have deeply confounded positional and semantic statistics — subject-verb pairs really do appear at characteristic distances in English, so a feature that looks semantic under in-distribution tests may still be a positional artifact that generalizes because the positional regularity is nearly universal in the training data; the only real escape is out-of-distribution generalization to typologically different languages or artificially constructed formal languages where the positional statistics are scrambled by design, as in work using SCAN or CFQ-style compositional generalization benchmarks. Concretely, you'd want to evaluate the factored SAE on code (where binding — variable declaration to use — has completely different positional statistics than natural language coreference) and on a synthetic language with free word order, and a feature that survives both transfers with stable activation geometry is much more credibly encoding the semantic relationship rather than its positional shadow.

response:
The empirical picture from attention head analysis suggests neither clean sharing nor pure idiosyncrasy, but a structured redundancy with functional specialization: work on GPT-2 by Elhage et al. and the "In-context Learning and Induction Heads" paper identifies clusters of heads that perform similar operations (induction, previous-token, copying) with highly correlated attention patterns, yet each head's value matrix projects onto a different subspace of d_model, meaning two heads can route identically but write different content to the residual stream — so a factored SAE would recover similar (query-key) binding geometry across heads in a cluster but different content directions in the d_model component, which is a precise decomposition of what "redundant but not identical" means mechanistically. If binding features form a coherent shared basis across heads, the implication is that concept binding is a residual stream phenomenon: the heads are interchangeable instruments writing to a shared representational space, and the binding feature lives in the residual stream's geometry rather than in any individual head, which would mean you could ablate any single head in the cluster and binding would degrade gracefully — consistent with the "majority vote" redundancy observed when ablating induction heads in GPT-2 medium, where single-head ablation causes ~15-20% performance drop rather than catastrophic failure. If instead each head develops idiosyncratic feature geometry, binding is a head-internal phenomenon, and the apparent redundancy is an illusion created by similar behavioral outputs masking different internal representations — this would imply that the correct unit of analysis for binding is the full (head, layer) pair, not the residual stream, and that interventions need to be head-specific to be interpretable. The most likely true answer, suggested by the virtual weights / composition score framework, is hierarchical: within a functional cluster (say, the 3-4 induction heads in GPT-2 large), the (query-key) routing component of binding features shares a basis, but the value-space content directions are orthogonal across heads by construction since attention concatenates heads before projecting — meaning binding detection is shared but binding content-writing is partitioned, and a factored SAE that doesn't separately handle these two components will conflate them. The deepest implication is that concept binding probably doesn't "live" in any single computational object but is enacted through a circuit where routing (shared across heads) and content-writing (head-specific) are separable, and the SAE geometry question dissolves into a circuit-finding question — which suggests that factored SAEs trained on individual heads are the wrong unit and the right object is an SAE on the composed output of a head cluster after the output projection matrix W_O has mixed them back into the residual stream.

response:
Feature geometry in the sense of "cosine similarity between decoder directions in a fixed basis" does become ill-defined across a multi-layer circuit, because each layer's residual stream lives in the same nominal d_model-dimensional space but the effective subspace that the circuit uses rotates and translates as information is processed — what Anthropic's work on residual stream as a "communication channel" implicitly acknowledges is that the same direction in R^{d_model} means something different at layer 4 versus layer 12, so comparing feature directions across layers without accounting for the layer-specific linear transformations is like comparing compass bearings in two different coordinate systems and calling the numerical equality meaningful. Persistent homology is a genuinely attractive replacement because it is basis-independent and captures topological features of the activation manifold — connected components, loops, voids — that persist across the filtration parameter, and if a binding circuit carves out a consistent manifold shape across layers (say, a torus corresponding to two independently varying bound concepts), that topological signature would be stable under the layer-to-layer rotations that break geometric comparisons; work by Chaudhuri, Guss, and others on neural manifold topology and more recently Henighan et al.'s unpublished explorations of representation geometry suggest this is computationally feasible for d_model ~ 512-1024 with Vietoris-Rips complexes on ~10k activation samples. The concrete problem with persistent homology for circuits specifically is the filtration alignment problem: persistent homology gives you a summary of the manifold at each layer independently, but a binding circuit is a dynamic object where the manifold at layer L+1 is shaped by computations at layer L, and standard TDA tools don't have a canonical way to track which topological feature at layer L "becomes" which feature at layer L+1 — you'd need something like a persistent homology morphism or a sheaf-theoretic construction over the layer poset, which exists in the math (MacPherson and Patel's persistent local systems, or Curry's sheaves on posets) but has essentially no practical implementation at transformer scale. A more tractable middle ground is linear representation hypothesis stress-testing via circuit-conditioned probes: rather than full TDA, you identify the circuit's active components via path patching, freeze those components, and ask whether a linear probe trained on the layer-L activations conditioned on the circuit being active recovers a stable feature direction across layers — if it does, linear feature geometry is still a valid local description of the circuit's representational strategy even if it fails globally, which is the implicit assumption behind most current mechanistic interpretability work and worth making explicit as a testable claim. The honest answer is that "feature geometry" is probably best understood not as a single well-defined object but as a scale-dependent description: at the level of individual SAE features within a layer it's well-defined and useful, at the level of cross-layer circuit analysis it needs augmentation with transport operators (Jacobians) or topological tools, and at the level of the full model it may need to be abandoned in favor of causal/interventional descriptions entirely — and the field hasn't yet produced a unified framework that works cleanly at all three scales simultaneously.

The gold standard evidence would be interventional predictive validity: if the sheaf's consistency maps genuinely capture the model's computations, then intervening on the activation at layer L in the direction specified by the consistency map's predicted transport should produce a predictable and specific change at layer L+k — not just any change, but the change that the sheaf predicts, with other directions held approximately fixed. Concretely, you'd take a binding circuit (say, the coreference resolution circuit in a GPT-2-scale model), construct the sheaf over layers 4-8, use the consistency map to predict what a ±ε perturbation of the "antecedent entity" feature at layer 4 should look like at layer 7, then perform activation patching and measure whether the actual layer-7 activation change aligns with the sheaf's prediction to within some tolerance — a sheaf that predicts the direction of change with cosine similarity >0.8 and the magnitude within 20% across a held-out set of sentences would be strong evidence, while a sheaf that predicts direction but not magnitude, or neither, is just curve-fitting. A second critical test is counterfactual coherence under circuit lesioning: if you ablate one component of the circuit (say, zero out a specific attention head's output), the sheaf's consistency maps over the remaining components should degrade in a structured way — the global section should become inconsistent at the ablated node, with the inconsistency (measured as the coboundary of the section) localizing precisely to the heads downstream of the ablation rather than diffusing everywhere, which would demonstrate that the sheaf's topology mirrors the circuit's causal topology rather than being a global smoothing artifact. The failure mode an expert worries about is expressivity without specificity: sheaf constructions are flexible enough that you can almost always fit a sheaf with low inconsistency to any activation data after the fact, analogous to how you can always fit a high-degree polynomial to noisy data — the real test is whether the sheaf fitted on one distribution of inputs (say, English coreference) transfers its consistency maps to a structurally similar but distributionally different task (say, variable binding in Python code), because genuine capture of computational structure should generalize while post-hoc fitting should not. The deepest evidentiary bar, which no current interpretability method has fully cleared, is synthesis: use the sheaf's global sections to construct a new input that should activate the binding circuit in a specific predicted configuration, then verify that the model's actual activations match the sheaf's prediction for that constructed input — this is the difference between a map that describes territory and a map you can navigate with, and clearing that bar for a sheaf construction would be genuinely novel evidence that the mathematical structure is doing real explanatory work.
